reflexion_entries_to_archive.text: S139 P1: S138 shipped damageEntity as 'the ONE way anything in the world takes damage' - typed, serialized, hashed, 22 passing tests, a docblock stating the contract, and a handoff recording the blocker as GONE. A.0 found it had ZERO production call sites. The only importer in the entire repo was its own test file, while three live damage paths went on calling damageCreature directly. It was correct, tested, dead code for a full session. The reason no test caught it is the important part: all 22 unit tests called damageEntity THEMSELVES, so every one passed while the game never invoked it once. The defect was not in the function's behaviour, it was the ABSENCE OF AN EDGE from the game to the function - a property of the import graph, which no behavioural test can see. Two durable lessons. (a) 'Shipped' means called, not merely present and green; a new dispatcher's acceptance criterion must include a named production caller. (b) When a claim is about reachability, the guard has to read the import graph - damage.wired.test.ts is a filesystem scan for exactly that reason, and it strips comments first so a docblock mentioning the symbol cannot masquerade as a call site.

S139 P1: the obvious lock test was PRIMITIVE_MAX_HP === 1000. That would have been nearly worthless. The number is not load-bearing as a number - it is load-bearing because 1%, 2.5% and 5% of it are INTEGERS, which is what makes damageEntity's integer guard unfireable at runtime. Pinning the value still permits someone to 'improve' it to 1024 and silently destroy that property. So the tests assert the RELATIONSHIPS: the percentages land on integers, DOT_CADENCE_TICKS === 0.5*PHYSICS_HZ, and attackFireTick === chewHits * CHEW_INTERVAL_TICKS for every chewing config. That last one existed ONLY as a comment ('chewHits: 5, // = constants.ts CHEW_HITS') beside two hardcoded literals, and A.0b measured that breaking it makes the sever dispatch never fire - the chew caps forever with the bond intact. Generalisation: when you lock a constant, first ask what PROPERTY makes it correct, and lock that. Also add a non-vacuity assertion (chewers.length > 0), or a future refactor that empties the collection turns the guard green and silent.

R3_goblin_model.reading: This REPLACES the amendment's model entirely. The three units are no longer three recipe-anchored DefenderKinds. The new model is a PRODUCER/UNIT split: (a) TWO goblin TOWERS (melee + ranged) are emplacements built from small recipes; (b) feeding a tower 3 primitives produces ONE goblin UNIT; (c) primitives come from the castle bank via the shipped PULL_FROM_BANK -> porch -> place path; (d) goblin UNITS walk out and attack the nearest enemy structure, or each other; (e) 6 attacks destroys a connector (bond) or a unit; (f) every player is granted one goblin of each kind free at match start.
R3_goblin_model.consequence_dissolved: Amendment 2b Q3 (does defender death raze its anchor - wrong for a unit?) is DISSOLVED, not answered. Under the producer model the goblin is not anchored to a recipe primitive at all: the TOWER owns the anchor, the UNIT is spawned. So there is no anchor to raze when a unit dies, and no immortal-defender re-mint risk for units. The re-mint concern now applies only to the towers, where razing the anchor is the correct shipped behaviour anyway.
R3_goblin_model.consequence_substrate: CANDIDATE SUBSTRATE SHIFT, being verified in A.0b before any design rests on it: units look like CREATURES, not Defenders. Creatures already spawn from spawners, walk, carry targetBondId AND targetCreatureId as parallel nullable fields, have hp, and already destroy bonds via chewProgress against CHEW_HITS=5 (owner says 6). If that holds, the redesign rides shipped machinery instead of extending the defender FSM - and the A.0 finding that new DefenderKinds silently render as nothing and silently drift (neither pinned nor frozen) stops applying to the units.
R3_goblin_model.open_cost: 6 attacks needs a home: A.0b must establish whether chewProgress is strictly per-attacker (so two goblins on one bond do not share progress) or whether the counter must move onto the bond.

Ordering rationale, which is not merely budgetary: the Council's decisive R1 finding was that the Stink Tower shipped alone is an INERT PROP because nothing in the game can attack a defender. The goblin is the thing that makes damage real. Shipping the goblin first therefore means the tower lands next session into a world that can already fight it, which is the correct dependency order regardless of context. The goblin also stands alone as playable new gameplay (units that raid enemy structures), whereas the tower does not.
